newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. Security Council supports new Congo probe.
newsitem.headline: U.N. Security Council supports new Congo probe.

text.p: The Security Council on Tuesday supported a new U.N. mission to investigate alleged massacres in the former eastern Zaire, although it expressed "wide disappointment" at President Laurent Kabila's stance.

Council President Peter Osvald of Sweden said it was important to uncover the truth about the killings "not only for a future national reconciliation of the Democratic Republic of the Congo but also for the future international relations with the country."

Kabila, who turned down a probe by the U.N. Commission for Human Rights into the killings of Rwandan Hutu refugees, is in danger of losing foreign assistance if he blocks the new mission to be organised by U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan.
Osvald said there was "wide disappointment" among council members on the Congo's response to the original probe. But he said Annan "has the support of the Council for his mission."

Annan and the United States, especially its embassy in Rwanda, have been accused of giving in to Kabila's demand to replace the original Geneva-based human rights commission team of experts, thereby delaying the mission further and raising concerns that evidence can be destroyed in the interim. The United Nations says about 200,000 refugees are missing.

The Kabila government, a rebel movement that ousted Zairean President Mobutuo Sese Seko in May, has objected to human rights investigator Roberto Garreton of Chile and asked for 10 days' notice of the names of the investigators.
Annan said it was important to establish the truth quickly, and his team would leave as soon as possible.
"Garreton is not the issue. I plead with you ... please don't talk in terms of who has won and who has lost and who caved in and who has not caved in," he said.

"The issues are much more important. I think we owe those who have lost relatives. We owe it to send a powerful message to the world that this kind of behaviour will not be tolerated," he told reporters after briefing the council.

Garreton visited the country briefly in March and concluded there was enough evidence to warrant a full investigation of massacres. He had a list of about 40 sites from eyewitnesses but Kabila contends Garreton came to conclusions before he was able to actually conduct a probe.
Kabila also wants the probe to cover the years before his rebels and Rwandan troops were engaged against the refugees and Annan indicated that would probably be done.
"It is not inconceivable that when the investigators begin to dig, they will find bodies who were killed this year, last year, in 1994," he said.
Human rights groups as well as some diplomats fear a precedent is being created that allows a country to choose its own team without suffering the consequences of isolation.

"Don't assume the mission is going to stop the massacres without putting pressure on where the pressure belongs -- which is on the government of Rwanda, which is in control of the troops, and by Kabila asserting his authority as the true president of the whole country," said Felice Gaer of the Jacob Blaustein Institute and a sometimes U.S. human rights envoy.

Asked about the criticism, U.N. spokesman Fred Eckhard said the human rights commission "when faced with unacceptable conditions found itself stymied. It had the option of redefining its mandate and the composition but it chose instead to pass the ball to the secretary-general.
"So he is out to achieve the same objective with a different cast of characters," he added.
